📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we all know the story of GTA 5 making more than $1 billion in the first three days it was on sale, right? At the time, Take-Two believed this to be the fastest any entertainment property had achieved the impressive milestone - music and films included. It made history, and with ease. And it looks like GTA 6 is going to do even better.

At least, that's according to one analyst, Joost van Dreunen, a senior data analyst and great writer/numbers diviner who wrote some predictions in his respected SuperJoost PlayList newsletter. "My prediction: Take-Two announces opening-weekend sales above $2 billion by Monday, 23rd November," he wrote. And you know what? I reckon he's onto something.

Let's review what we already know: there is a conservative estimate of 10 million pre-orders for Rockstar's latest game floating around - something buoyed by comments from Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick - and, even by the tech giant's lofty expectations, we know the game is tracking "well above expectations" when it comes to pre-orders.

In a recent development, we also know a lot of people are shelling out for the slightly more pricey Ultimate Edition (£90). So many people are opting for the more expensive version, in fact, that Take-Two revised its financial forecast up to $3.5bn for the next financial quarter, thanks to "recurrent consumer spending" (something Zelnick clarified in an investor's call is explicitly linked to the Ultimate Edition). 10 million pre-orders, at roughly $100 per copy - that's $1 billion right off the bat.

Sources indicate that "That’s two days faster than its predecessor," van Dreunen said, "and largely before anyone has even played the game." That other $1bn will come over the weekend. And then, per the analyst, the game will sell roughly another 28 million copies over the course of the first year it's on sale. "My forecast puts first-year sales at 38 million copies, only modestly ahead of GTA 5’s 35 million. The real difference may be how much revenue each player generates over the years that follow.".

It has been revealed that but it's what follows in the newsletter that intrigues me most. "At the high end, [GTA 6] may just lift the entire industry with it," wrote van Dreunen. "In the face of AI slop and shitty mobile games that exist only to extract revenue, it will offer a reprieve. At a time when the industry is increasingly focused on making games cheaper and monetising players more aggressively, Rockstar is about to demonstrate the enduring appeal of spending a fortune to make something people actually want to play.".

So, even if you're dubious about the game and Rockstar's motivations for selling as many copies as possible, the launch of GTA 6 could be something that gives the industry a much-needed jolt of life, in the face of rampant layoffs and shrinking talent pools.

It has been revealed that it's not all sunshine and rainbows ahead for Rockstar, though: amongst the frenzy of launch activity, Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion will be determined this week, as the game goes on sale.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One half of GTA 6's leading couple, Jason Duval, is unusually reserved and soft-spoken when compared to many of the crime series' boisterous, sometimes gleefully violent protagonists. Why the change? Rockstar Games' narrative lead notes the idea came from 1972's The Getaway and Jason's military background.

"When we decided we wanted to tell a story about a couple on the run, we looked at all the similar kinds of movies, and one of the ones that really stood out was [Sam] Peckinpah's The Getaway," senior vice president of narrative, Rupert Humphries, notes in a statement given to Destructoid.

It has been revealed that the crime flick's star Steve McQueen "was famous for pulling lines out of scripts and saying things with his presence alone," Humphries continues, and that's an energy the team at Rockstar wanted to somewhat match with Jason's characterisation. Although, he also acknowledges that "so many of our protagonists have been the opposite." Think Trevor and the like.

Recent findings suggest that "This also resonated with the research we were doing around veterans and particularly former Army Rangers (in our world we call them Marauders). These guys typically aren't running their mouths or reacting to something unless it's strictly necessary, while still being strong and still asserting themselves," Humphries adds.

The game itself definitely plays on those ideas, too. (Something noted in our GTA 6 review.) Jason isn't the most forthcoming or chatty protagonist, but what he leaves unsaid and when he chooses to communicate is just as vital as what he actually shares with Lucia - the other, more chaotic half of the game's central couple, who balances things out somewhat.

"Researching the prolific and headline-grabbing criminal activity that had been taking place over decades in Florida was an obvious starting point," game writer Michael Wiafe also noted of the game's sweeping story. "From then on, it was about coming up with authentic characters that didn't stray too far from reality but also were not totally bound by it either. The majority of our main characters are undeniably reprehensible on paper, full-blown criminals, but also decent human beings. Their moral makeup isn't necessarily cut-and-dry, and we don't attempt to make excuses for them. What's key is how they resonate, no matter where you're experiencing the game in the world.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A hacker has pleaded guilty to a number of online crimes, including the 2022 breach of Rockstar Games which resulted in a bunch of mid-development clips of GTA 6 in action leaking onto the net.

The BBC report that, on November 16th, Arion Kurtaj pleaded guilty at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar Games hack and a number of others he carried out with the hacking gang Lapsus$ while aged 16 and 17. Kurtaj, now aged 21, was previously sentenced to stay in a secure hospital indefinitely due to the severity of his autism, but was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial. He'll be sentenced at a later date.

Sources indicate that kurtaj carried out the 2022 Rockstar hack while on bail for other hacking offences and being housed at a Travelodge hotel under police protection, the latter on account of rival hackers threatening to attack him over stolen Bitcoin stashes. The Rockstar hack was reportedly done using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into the hotel room's TV, plus a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.

Sources indicate that 90 clips of unfinished GTA 6 were flung online by that hack, with Rockstar having refused to cooperate with Kurtaj's demand via an internal Slack channel that the manufacturer contact him on massaging app Telegram within 24 hours. Rockstar claimed the breach cost them $5m million to recover from, in addition to staff having to waste thousands of hours.

Sources indicate that earlier this year, GTA 6 suffered yet another leak, with a hacker or hackers going by "Cyberleek" posting various videos of the game in action. Rockstar and parent manufacturer Take-Two quickly sprung into action, taking down videos, filing subpoenas, and issuing a statement that called the leak "heartbreaking".

In a recent development, hopefully with the game's console release later this week, those will be the only two GTA 6 leaks which have to be added to the annals of gaming history. As much as marketing can leave a bad taste in the mouth, especially when it barely shows anything of the actual product being advertised, neither of the GTA 6 leaks served much of a purpose beyond forcing people to waste some time and energy talking about the perpetrators.

  • Online marketplace Etsy is facing backlash from people over a recent change to its policies that allow it and other companies to use content created by sellers to train AI models.
  • That seems pretty straightforward—anything you put on your Etsy page can be fed into the AI theft machine like Steve Buscemi in a Cohen Brothers film—and as reported by Cartoon Brew, it led to significant pushback from some Etsy users, including numerous store closures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Revision: Etsy told the Fresh York Times on Friday that it intends to revise the policy.

Online marketplace Etsy is facing backlash from people over a recent change to its policies that allow it and other companies to use content created by sellers to train AI models. In response, numerous vendors have closed their online shops, and are encouraging others to do the same. Etsy, however, notes the newly introduced policy isn't meant to "replace your creativity," but simply to improve storefront operations.

That seems pretty straightforward—anything you put on your Etsy page can be fed into the AI theft machine like Steve Buscemi in a Cohen Brothers film—and as reported by Cartoon Brew, it led to significant pushback from some Etsy users, including numerous store closures.

You might have heard of Etsy's upcoming terms and artists fleeing the platform. We're out, too.

Ring Cats Etsy final closure notice.

A post shared by Aaron Millard (@aaronmillardillustration).

In the wake of that reaction, Etsy vice president of customer operations James Ossman posted a separate update saying it's not really like that at all, and that "we do not use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity.".

In a recent development, "When we describe how we may use your content, we're enabling actions like translating your listing descriptions so buyers around the world can discover your items, or featuring your listing photos in Etsy marketing campaigns to showcase your creative work," Ossman wrote. "We also use your content to develop tools that make running your shop easier, like listing optimization tools or stats summaries that help you better understand your shop's performance. As always, your needs and feedback help guide how we build and improve these tools.".

As for providing third-party access to that content, Ossman said that too is for "services and tools that can help you run your business," and promised that "when we partner with third parties, we do so thoughtfully to help protect your content and data.".

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

In a recent development, that hasn't satisfied everyone. Ossman's commitment doesn't exist within the actual terms of service, which as seen above states only that Etsy and partners can "use Your Content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies." Ossman also noted in his enhancement that the terms "prohibit scraping Etsy or unauthorized use of content from Etsy to train AI models," but that (as far as I can tell) applies to Etsy people and unauthorized third-parties, not Etsy itself or those it licenses.

It has been revealed that that's not to suggest that Etsy is being underhanded, merely that the binding legal language is imprecise. Others also complain that AI training should be opt-in rather than on by default—and worse, there's apparently no opt-out option available at all, so people who are opposed to having their work used for AI training for any reason are out of luck.

Ironically, the blowup over Etsy's embrace of AI training comes just weeks after it earned plaudits for banning AI-generated recipes and patterns, a move Ossman mentioned was necessary to establish "trust" in the platform: "Sellers need clear guidance and confidence that their creativity and craftsmanship will be represented fairly; buyers need to understand what they’re buying and the human involvement behind it.".

However this ultimately shakes out, the Etsy AI backlash is emblematic of a growing problem on both sides of the buy-sell divide: People want refuge from the creeping tendrils of the AI behemoth, and overtly or insidiously it's becoming increasingly difficult to find one. The more that happens, the more people are likely to react forcefully when platforms like Etsy start edging in the direction, regardless of any promises (or even carved-in-legal-stone commitments) of good intentions.

I've reached out to Etsy to ask if the newly introduced AI policy might be changed in response to the complaints and closures, and will update if I receive a reply.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mainstay of the GTA series has been the presence of sex workers, but Rockstar Games has dropped this aspect for the newly released GTA 6.

As reported by Shack News, unlike most other games in the long-running franchise, you cannot hire a sex worker in GTA 6.

The outlet asked Rockstar about this decision, and received the following response:.

According to recent reports, "GTAVI is a game about a couple in a bind, lovers on the run. While we have taken a lot forward from previous GTA titles, everything we have implemented in VI has been done to support the spirit of the story we wanted to tell, and the gameplay systems we wanted to expand upon - things like wanted system, the radio, robberies and car theft. Many aspects of previous titles are not present in GTAVI, but the elements we have we believe are all necessary and complementary to the feeling and motivations we wanted to emphasize as you play through Jason and Lucia's story.".

So, in other words, sex workers aren't included this time around because it wouldn't make sense for Jason or Lucia to pursue that, as they're already in a relationship — and that's a substantial part of the story.

As mentioned, they have been present in the series since 2001's GTA 3, and this will be the first 3D game to exclude them.

Industry observers note that GTA 6 is also the first game that centres on a couple, however, with the relationship between Jason and Lucia interwoven in the gameplay as well as being a key tenet of the narrative. It seems Rockstar didn't think sex workers would be conducive to this goal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You may have recently read that CD Projekt Red's in-development Cyberpunk 2 may be trying to revive the original game's online ambitions. But, if you don't want to wait the many years it'll likely be before the Cyberpunk 2077 sequel arrives, then I've got good news for you: Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer mod CyberMP is now out in open beta.

"After almost six years of development, countless reworks, and code rewrites, we're finally launching the public beta," the modders on the CyberMP Discord channel wrote (thanks RPS). "Anyone can jump in and play now - no invites or applications needed." The team notes, however, that this is "true beta", meaning "Crashes, desyncs, and server drops under heavy load are completely normal for now. That's exactly why we need testers.".

Alongside the potential shakiness, the devs say it's also possible the mod could ping your anti-virus software, since it "doesn't have a digital signature yet". Whilst the priorities for the team lie in "polishing the foundations" and "fixing crashes and stability", more features are eventually planned. But for now, they stress, "let's see how the project handles real player traffic!".

So, what exactly is it? CyberMP is a dedicated multiplayer modification for Cyberpunk 2077 that allows you and your friends to explore Night City together: drive vehicles, engage in combat, and play custom community-created game modes on high-tick dedicated servers. You need an official copy of the game to play it (obviously), and the mod is completely free to download. You can download the mod, and read a fair amount of how to get it working, what to expect from it, and how to troubleshoot any issues, over at its dedicated website.

In a recent development, if you're thinking 'Hang on, why does Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer sound so familiar?', it's because the game was supposed to receive an official multiplayer mode after its original release. Thanks to its shaky launch, however, plans changed, and CD Projekt Red later declared that multiplayer would be a separate "triple-A release", but, eventually, that too was cancelled. The studio is still keen to honour the idea, though, and recently stated it's "focusing on bringing online into all of our franchises one day".

According to recent reports, this isn't the first big bit of news we've had about Cyberpunk 2077 mods this week. Just yesterday, a newly introduced mod called 'Torrent' added 3D rain, lightning storms, and tyre spray to Night City - all rendered and made lovely with a new lighting system that seems to play nicely with other weather mods that have been created for the game.

Persona 5 – in its original state – released over a decade ago on 15th September 2016, and although Persona 6 has now been officially confirmed, we're none the wiser as to when it will actually come out.

It's likely to finally land at some point in 2027 after the dust has settled from Persona 4 Revival, but according to a recent interview with general producer Kazuhisa Wada (thanks, Nintendo Everything), fans won't have to wait quite so long for the inevitable Persona 7.

Sources indicate that "We will continue to cherish what makes Persona unique, while also embracing changes in the times and needs, and taking on latest challenges. We aim to be a brand that can grow for 5, 10 years, and beyond.

"And Persona 6 is not the end. We are working on various things to ensure that you don’t have to wait as long for the next installment as we have in the past. And in order to make Persona an even bigger IP, we are constantly thinking about creative ideas and developments that will not disappoint your expectations. Please look forward to what’s to come from Persona.”.

It has been revealed that we will look forward to it, Wada-san, thank you sir. Let's keep the focus on Persona 4 Revival and Persona 6 for now though, hm?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that tech giant Intel are being taken to court for allegedly "misleading" their investors about the sheer scale of the impact of generative AI-fuelled component price hikes on PC sales.
  • All this follows Intel's last round of quarterly results, in which they revealed a significant revenue fall; this triggered an Intel stock price drop from $92.07 per share on October 29th to $65.76 per share the next day, which this week's lawsuit characterises as "the largest single-day price decline for Intel common stock in over 50 years".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that tech giant Intel are being taken to court for allegedly "misleading" their investors about the sheer scale of the impact of generative AI-fuelled component price hikes on PC sales. The class action lawsuit in question claims that Intel's distribution and manufacturing partners have had to deal with "a massive glut of unwanted PC inventory", and that the gains from Intel's investments in AI datacenters aren't enough to make up for slowing sales of PCs to regular Josephines who just want fancy boxes they can play Deadlock on.

All this follows Intel's last round of quarterly results, in which they revealed a significant revenue fall; this triggered an Intel stock price drop from $92.07 per share on October 29th to $65.76 per share the next day, which this week's lawsuit characterises as "the largest single-day price decline for Intel common stock in over 50 years".

Sources indicate that the lawyers in question are from Robbins LLP, who specialise in "shareholder, whistleblower, antitrust, & consumer litigation". In a press release, they say they've filed suit on behalf of anybody who bought Intel stock from July 23rd to October 29th this year.

The suit claims that Intel neglected to tell investors that falling PC and component sales were having a "materially greater negative impact" on their third financial quarter 2026 Client Computing and Physical AI Groupresults than Intel had previously stated – to the tune of "hundreds of millions of dollars" in revenue shrinkage, compared to the previous quarter, with the situation still expected to "worsen".

They also accuse the organization of keeping schtum about the aforesaid "massive glut of unwanted PC inventory", together with the fact that "any positive impacts to Intel’s business and financial results resulting from data center construction and other aspects of the AI boom were more than offset by the negative effects on the Company’s business and financial results resulting from the PC market slowdown and the excess inventory buildup described above.".

Finally, they say Intel bosses have failed to disclose that they're struggling to procure an adequate supply of substrates – that is, materials used to create the base layer of chips, circuit boards and similar components. As such, the lawyers claim, Intel couldn't "ramp up production to meet data center CPU demand even if the Tech giant chose to divert production resources because of a slowdown in PC-related sales.".

Once the Godzilla of personal computing, Intel haven't been having a brilliant few years. Back in 2024, they recorded a multi-billion dollar quarterly loss, pushing then-CEO Pat Gelsinger to resign. As regards sales of gaming PCs, they've fallen behind AMD, though they've reportedly taken some ground back recently as regards desktop CPUs. According to recent reports, with the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever there's a whole latest world filled with niche gear and strange baubles to collect. But one item in particular has drawn the ire of the creators of a popular completionist add-on.

Sources indicate that that add-on is All the Things, a must-install for collectors like me, as it acts as a database of all the gear, mounts, titles, crafting recipes, and super rare drops in the game. Once you collect something, it is hidden in the add-on, thus tracking your progress and making for a fantastic tool for picking the game apart.

In a recent development, on occasion, specific items have written notes attached by the All the Things development team, as is true of a special World of Warcraft: Forever toy, the Pouch of Violet Dust. This is a promotional item that was obtainable by watching two hours of WoW Forever streams between the 4th and 12th November.

Recent findings suggest that it's a powerful toy! When used on a campfire, it changes the fire's colour to purple and extends the buffs provided by it from the usual one hour to two hours. But the sticking point with the item isn't its existence, rather the fact that it's going to be removed in early December, not long from now.

This is what the creators of the All the Things add-on don't like. "A week-long, Twitch-only window for an item that gets taken away a month later is exactly the kind of FOMO that disheartens collectors," the creators mentioned in a note attached to the item in the mod. "It can't be earned by playing the game at all. Even those who get it don't get to keep it.".

Industry observers note that they aren't alone in feeling this way. Comments below the item's listing on the Wowhead database are equally scorching. "I love FOMO in their explicitly non-fomo game," wrote user TheWhiteRose.

"Just... Why?" added user Darrenic427. "They could very easily just patch out the camp buff duration and keep the visual effect, but Blizzard just doesn't like pretty fire I guess. Figures that they finally give us access to purple fire but then take it away after a month.".

Industry observers note that the battle between collectors and time-limited FOMO items is one that has been waged for about as long as these sorts of items have been a part of games. Though for the pouch, it's an especially weird case: an item that's cool to have but so temporary in nature that it makes it both key to completionists and strangely pointless to care about. Whether it makes a return in a later update for World of Warcraft: Forever and doesn't require out-of-game actions to obtain, and doesn't disappear, we'll have to wait and see.

According to recent reports, woW Forever itself is proving popular among players - me included. It's added a staggering amount of upcoming quests and many new features to the original version of World of Warcraft, which, in turn, has injected the game with an impressive amount of new items to collect. Completionists will likely be glued to the game for a long time.

#86554. Tech Report: Each new GTA moves the series closer and closer to the original Mafia, the open-world game that bettered Rockstar

Tech Report: Each new GTA moves the series closer and closer to the original Mafia, the open-world game that bettered Rockstar

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (921 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This week sees the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, the open-world crime 'em up that's been in development for at least eight years and has been waited on by fans for even longer.
  • Released less than a year after Grand Theft Auto 3, Mafia is perhaps a more prescient example of Rockstar's future than their own.
  • Set in Lost Heaven, a shoe-in for 1930s Chicago, Illinois, you play through Tommy Angelo's rise from a taxi driver, who has a chance run in with the Salieri crime family, to one of the gang's main enforcers in their fight against their rivals, the Morellos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This week sees the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, the open-world crime 'em up that's been in development for at least eight years and has been waited on by fans for even longer. Naturally, over on PC we're still waiting for a port to be unveiled, let alone a release date to circle in our calendars. But, as happens whenever a new GTA is on the horizon, I think about Mafia: City of Lost Heaven.

Released less than a year after Grand Theft Auto 3, Mafia is perhaps a more prescient example of Rockstar's future than their own.

Set in Lost Heaven, a shoe-in for 1930s Chicago, Illinois, you play through Tommy Angelo's rise from a taxi driver, who has a chance run in with the Salieri crime family, to one of the gang's main enforcers in their fight against their rivals, the Morellos.

It has been revealed that the influences on developers Illusion Softworks are obviously cinematic, with whole sequences ripped from The Godfather films and Goodfellas (and I'd argue there's a sprinkling of Once Upon A Time In America for good measure). A habit they share with Rockstar, who also pull liberally from crime films that share the settings of their games. But Illusion Softworks are also clearly interested in capturing the history of the Prohibition era, too. The story begins in the aftermath of the 1929 Wall Street Crash and the depression that followed, running through until the late 30s, and you see that time pass in the city around you. Buildings that are under construction at the start of the game are completed by its end, a used car lot in Chinatown sits empty for most of the game until business picks up with the economy, but most enjoyable of all is that the cars driving the streets change. At first the roads are filled with Ford Model-T-inspired vehicles that basically look like horse carriages with engines, but by the end of the game they've all become much sleeker creatures that have left their early carriage influences behind.

The city Illusion Softworks built also has a dedication to verisimilitude that we see Rockstar adopting in their later games. As you drive Lost Heaven's streets, you must pay attention to speed limits and red lights, as speeding and running traffic lights will both earn you a fine if a policeman spots you. For fans of public transport, there are streetcars and overhead trams you can ride to navigate the city, too. Two other touches I love: when you reload your gun, you dump the whole clip instead of returning the unfired bullets to a magic ammo reservoir, and vehicles can run out of fuel if you drive them too far.

Much had been made of all the simulations running under the surface of Grand Theft Auto 6, such as fully realised cloud formation, a smell reaction system, and… fuel tanks that can run empty. No doubt they're significantly more impressive than what's on show in Mafia, and this isn't about putting the two games against each other (even if one of them was likely made for less than the other studio spent on coffee runs across its eight-year development). Nor is it about saying history recognised the wrong game: Grand Theft Auto 3 was a huge step forward in open-world gaming and Mafia was recognised and celebrated in its time. It's about something else.

Back in 2002, Illusion Softworks offered a different kind of open-world crime game. One that was more mature despite having a lower age rating. Grand Theft Auto was undoubtedly more influential, sparking imitators that mostly opted to follow its tone and sensibilities – Saints Row began in a similar place to GTA 3 and as the series continued leaned further into the silliness and parody, for instance. But while for many years Mafia stood as a sign to an open world path that could have been taken, the longer Grand Theft Auto series has gone on, the more Rockstar have found their way toward the example set by Illusion Softworks. The games are still aiming for bombastic comedy at times, but they're also interested in the likes of newly-arrived-in-America Niko Belic, or Michael de Santa, a retired criminal haunted by his past. They're much richer protagonists than Claude, the silent character you play in GTA 3.

The Mafia series has continued, marked by ideas that remain as interesting as what was on show in the original. In Mafia 3, you play Lincoln Clay, a black soldier returned from the war in Vietnam and brought into the family. Set in a take on New Orleans, Louisiana, during the civil rights movement, you face overt racism. Linger too long in white, wealthy neighbourhoods and the residents will call on the police to move you along. And the Definitive Edition remake of the first game, released in 2020, is a rare example of a game that both captures the spirit of the original and justifies its existence by expanding and bettering the story. Though I don't think any of its sequels have been as innovative, nor as forward thinking, as the first game.

According to recent reports, I don't want to come across as Rockstar-bashing. The studio have continued to push the open-world genre forward with every release and I want to see what other developers lift from GTA 6 for their own games. But I'm even more pleased that as the studio's aged, their work has grown closer to Illusion Softworks'.

Leader of the UK Conservative Party (and former Mortal Kombat player) Kemi Badenoch is more worried about the amount of time people will spend playing GTA 6 rather than the game itself.

Sources indicate that every fresh Grand Theft Auto game invites some amount of controversy over its in-game violence or depictions of sex and drugs - from San Andreas' raunchy Hot Coffee mini-game to GTA 5's graphic torture scene. Ahead of GTA 6's release this week, the Tory leader downplayed those fears.

"I would be more worried about the amount of time people were spending on a game than the game specifically. I remember in my childhood playing Mortal Kombat and Street Fighter. I didn't hit anybody after playing those games," Badenoch said in a news conference shared by Sky News (good spot, IGN).

It has been revealed that while Badenoch's stance might be surprising for the normally right-wing UK political party, she did still worry over children who might play GTA 6 for too long. There are probably far worse ways for kids to spend their time than engaging with a long-form story like GTA 6's, though, especially in an era with endless amounts of 10-second clips to mindlessly scroll past and declining funding into youth programs.

It has been revealed that "I haven't played Grand Theft Auto, I know people are worried about the game content. At the same time, I'd be more worried about a kid who played it all day, who was in their bedroom all day, than one who spends half an hour on it and then went out and did something else. They are two different things," Badenoch added.

It has been revealed that GTA 6's release is imminent and is expected to be the biggest entertainment launch of all time. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that one first-party title from the GameCube library that's well and truly outlived this particular Nintendo generation is Super Smash Bros. Melee, and today happens to be the game's 25th anniversary in Japan.

Industry observers note that after introducing fans to the series in 1999 on the N64, Masahiro Sakurai and the team at HAL Laboratory & Nintendo rolled out this new, improved, and faster take on the all-star Nintendo fighter in November 2001. Not only was it a popular couch game, but Melee went on to have an incredibly successful run as a competitive game.

According to Nintendo's official data, Melee is officially the "best-selling game of all time" for the GameCube, shifting over seven million copies worldwide, with the system itself selling 21.74 million units during its lifetime.

This particular entry was so influential within the Smash scene that it led to Nintendo re-releasing the GameCube controller and making newer entries in the series compatible with this same pad, as it was the preferred pick for any serious or pro player.

In a recent development, to this day, the game's competitive scene is still going strong, with game's meta continuing to evolve, and players like "Hungrybox" (the famous Jigglypuff main) are still knocking about. Of course, there have also been plenty of scandals within the competitive space over the years, but Melee continues to thrive, and is still capable of packing out events across the globe.

Sources indicate that so, on behalf of the team here at Nintendo Life, here's to another 25 years of duking it out. Oh, and if Nintendo hasn't already got something planned, now would be the perfect time to add Melee to the Switch 2's GameCube library. For North America, the game's 25th anniversary takes place in early December.

Feel free to share your memories of Smash Bros. Melee in the comments. Are you still playing it 25 years on? Let us know.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that some very rough napkin math led to estimates that Take-Two Interactive expected to make as much as $3.5 billion during the Grand Theft Auto 6 launch period. It actually made more than that on the GTA 6 launch day: Rockstar says the game pulled in $3.79 billion in "day one retail sales," making it "the biggest entertainment launch in history.".

Recent findings suggest that by way of comparison, Avengers: Endgame, ranked on Wikipedia as the highest grossing movie of all time, earned a little more than $2.9 billion over its entire theatrical run. GTA 6 crushed that by nearly $1 billion in a day.

"It is with immense gratitude that we enter a new chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of Grand Theft Auto 6," Rockstar Games president and co-founder Sam Houser said. "We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you.".

Strauss Zelnick, CEO of publisher Take-Two Interactive, had previously said that preorder levels of Grand Theft Auto 6 were "unprecedented" but declined to reveal specifics. It turns out he wasn't kidding: Take-Two Interactive also revealed today that GTA 6 sold 32.5 million copies in pre-release, which it said is "a latest record across all platforms.".

Those numbers are absolutely staggering: There was never any question that GTA 6 was going to be huge, but those launch days sales—sales from one single day—surpass Take Two's net revenue guidance for the entire quarter by nearly $400 million at the high end.

Given that there's still well over a month remaining in the holiday season, I'd expect that figure to rise significantly: I'm not an industry analyst but more than $4 billion before the year is over suddenly seems just about conservative. Beyond that, I won't even hazard a guess, but consider this: Grand Theft Auto 5, which sold a little over 11 million copies on its launch day in 2013, has now surpassed 230 million copies sold in total. The sky, to paraphrase one of Tom Petty's other songs, really is the limit.

Rockstar wants you to see yourself in GTA 6's Jason and Lucia

💡 Key Takeaways
  • GTA 6's Jason and Lucia might be hardened criminals, but Rockstar Games designed the couple to be relatable in other ways.
  • It has been revealed that "Playing GTA 6, the main thing we want players to feel is connection.
  • "Living in the actual world in this present moment, it feels like there is so much noise and so much pressure on everyone - politics, the environment, media, social media.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6's Jason and Lucia might be hardened criminals, but Rockstar Games designed the couple to be relatable in other ways. As the studio's narrative lead explained, "we are all about two bits of bad luck away from completely losing it" in the real world.

It has been revealed that "Playing GTA 6, the main thing we want players to feel is connection. To Jason and Lucia, who they need to believe in and inhabit for this journey through the game, but then also that connection in the game between the two characters," senior vice president of narrative, Rupert Humphries, explained in quotes given to GamesRadar+.

"Living in the actual world in this present moment, it feels like there is so much noise and so much pressure on everyone - politics, the environment, media, social media. It's coming at you from everywhere. It seems like we are all about two bits of bad luck away from completely losing it. That is the world we are showing you on the streets of Vice City and in the rest of Leonida - everyone's been driven to a kind of madness that comes out in lots of different ways, from conspiracy theories to self-help cults to get-rich-quick schemes and drug habits.".

According to recent reports, GTA 6's main couple doesn't exactly have many options outside of the criminal ones, and I think the game does a good job at giving them some real, personal, human stakes to ground it all - making their occasional robberies and murders a tad more understandable. As the couple indicates in the game, the world is stacked against them. They can't get ahead by playing by the rules.

Even so, GTA 6 still has an optimistic view on life in the modern era, which itself is a substantial departure from GTA 5's generally cynical world view: "With all that going on, we wanted to have two humans at the center of the story that the player can care about and see themselves in, and then this idea that maybe (however bad you are) we might all be better off when we're together and not going it alone.".

#86547. My murderous wine merchant whines for a chance at republican rule in Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion, which isn't only about the money

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

My murderous wine merchant whines for a chance at republican rule in Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion, which isn't only about the money

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the tentacles of my trade empire snake up towards France in the west, down towards Africa in the south, and off into Hungary in the east.
  • In a recent development, I’ve shed blood in its name, the blood of someone else named Marco no less.
  • It should, in theory, help that he’s my best mate, thanks to a well-timed feast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the tentacles of my trade empire snake up towards France in the west, down towards Africa in the south, and off into Hungary in the east. Yet, I still can’t reach out and grasp the throne that sits right in front of me. I’m Marco Sanudo, and the throne of the serene republic of Venice eludes me.

In a recent development, I’ve shed blood in its name, the blood of someone else named Marco no less. I’ve managed to avoid punishment for that crime, despite the fact it earned me a fiefdom to rule while I’ve tried to up my patrician score enough to be the lucky party the next time a ruling Doge dies in office (or runs out their 10 year term). Sadly, Doge Leonardo, the mysterious masked lord who’s had an iron grip on power since the first couple of old blokes to hold the position in this playthrough popped their clogs, is proving incredibly tough to oust.

It should, in theory, help that he’s my best mate, thanks to a well-timed feast. It certainly did in being granted a pardon for offing that other Marco, but not even that and a plague which infected nearly everyone in the realm aside from me have paved the way to Dogedom. In the meantime, I’ve striven to gain wealth and influence. I’ve worked up to having four trade routes running at once, with goods like wine, iron, and textiles flowing from market to market across southern Europe and bringing a steady supply of coin back to my Venetian estate. I’ve built trade posts at the extremities of my routes, giving me the option of starting from further afield and reaching new lands if the cash flow dries up closer to home.

This is where Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion has blended a bit with the game’s traditional feudal moneymaking to supercharge my coffers. The land holding I killed a dude for, the Proveditorate of Zara, means I’ve also had tax money from modern day Croatia to add to both my trade profits and the income my domicile generates on its own. I am, as the medieval kids say, minted.

Getting to the point of serious pocket clinkage is, as you might imagine given Silk and Silver’s focus on filling the game’s world with travelling merchant companies and wheeler-dealing republican patrician families, the beating heart of the expansion. A near-constant stream of notifications about prices of different goods I’m trying to hawk in different locations encourage me to regularly prune and re-work my routes so that max profits are being earned and no carrying capacity’s being wasted. The bubbling up of wars and plagues impacts prices in affected cities, making it a never-ending battle if you’re desperate to optimise everything within an inch of its life. I’ve found that degree of micromanagement unnecessary if the goal is just to keep a decent profit margin ticking over. Just remember to replace the trader assigned to a route if they die, recall them every few years so they don’t stress themselves to death, and check in every so often to re-evaluate whether you’re running goods that are suitably in demand.

According to recent reports, if you stick at it for a decent amount of time, with a certain type of good - alcohol or jewellery, for example - your expertise in dealing in them increases, making it easier to sell for better prices. Trade routes left running between the same markets also gain boons from being in place for a long time, offering a counterpoint to rejigging them every five seconds to wring out a few more coins. Most of my routes have run along a path that includes stops at four markets, with the occasional location boasting a monopoly I’ve bargained for with the local ruler, so I don’t have to worry about competition at every stop.

Recent findings suggest that when you’re playing as a merchant who isn’t locked into the ruling inner circle of a republic, making your routes as lengthy as possible is one of the three moneymaking areas your organization can specialise in. That first one’s caravaneering, and is the one I leant into in a non-Marco Sanudo playthrough. Beyond that, you can become an expert loan shark, lending cash to rulers or paying their ransoms in order to recoup interest and collect hooks you can use for favours. Manufacturing expensive artifacts that can be sold individually to collectors for a profit is the third option. The latter two I’ve only dabbled in a little bit as of writing, having earned enough gold mostly from caravanneering to buy the land containing the city with my home market and be anointed a Sheikh. So, beginning as a landless merchant is a nice alternative to Crusader Kings 3’s long-established wandering adventurer starting point, with both allowing you to work your way up from lowly serf to landed lordly dynasty in your location of choice.

If you’re after a more specific historical scenario, Silk and Silver has Guelphs and Ghibellines. This is where we find Marco Sanudo, as well as the other patrician family head I’ve played as thus far, Speronella Dalesmanni. The setup is that the Pope and the Holy Roman Emperor have had a bit of a tiff, essentially rooted in who should have certain powers, with different cities and powerful families in northern Italy taking either the Guelph (Pope-likers) or Ghibelline (Holy Roman Empire-enjoyers) side depending on what suits their goals or principles. I’ll be honest, aside from being another way to easily earn friends or enemies in the ruthless crucible of merchant republican politics, where votes and reputation-bolstering aid from other nobles are key, the situation’s not had a hugely obvious bearing on my playthroughs thus far.

I think the closest it’s come is during my Dalesmanni run, if largely due to the existence of the By God Alone expansion allowing a newly introduced branch of Catholicism, dubbed Italian Christianity, to be created. The initial conversion push from the bishop responsible led a number of my fellow northern Italian nobles away from the Roman Rite headed by his Popeliness, making the Guelph/Ghibelline split more clearly defined.

In a recent development, in the early hours of both my Sanudo and Dalesmanni playthroughs, I’ve been far more focused on simply trying to push the respective patrician families up the hill from posh toffs with naught but a vote and a manor to elected rulers of their great cities, with land holdings to match. Speronella’s situation in Padua is made incredibly tough by the fact she’s a woman in a world where every succession rule is designed to put blokes first, so I’ve had more success with Marco and his quest to become the Doge of Venice.

Sources indicate that as the head of a patrician family, one of select few elite clans who steer the oligarchical republic, I was faced with earning Marco enough respect among his fellow family heads that they’d consider voting him to the top of the succession list, thus securing his power whenever the current Doge got the boot. Pulling that off, while also not kowtowing to the requests and schemes of those same peers, isn’t easy. A large cocktail of factors go into determining whether another noble likes you enough to vote in support of your succession. There’s your patrician rating, which is upped by doing things which specifically show you to be good at this Italian noble house lark, such as establishing trade monopolies for the republic, gaining the Pope’s favour, or having close relatives who also hold key positions in the republic. However, how close a friendship you have with the target and how their character traits align with you also play a huge rule.

According to recent reports, thus it was that, at one point, Marco was best mates with the current Doge and had a decent patrician rating, but had only amassed 68 of the 72 points needed for said Doge to vote for him because the Doge was generous, and therefore didn’t care for Marco’s ambitiousness. That same Doge either liked or respected Marco enough to grant him a council position and the status of regent, but he would not back Marco to replace him permanently for love nor money. This is the same man who liked Marco so much that when I pulled off that not-so-sneaky murder on another noble house head in order to inherit the keys to the Proveditorate of Zara, the Doge was instantly willing to pardon me and prevent Marco suffering any punishment for the crime.

Not even a couple of serious plagues hitting Venice, which at one point had all three people ahead of Marco in the queue suffering from smallpox, could get him on that throne. Eventually, it took a bit of lucky timing when his Doge mate died of old age - a few years after beating smallpox - to finally install Marco as Doge. Given that delayed promotion, as of writing I’ve not yet had enough time in the substantial chair to give a proper verdict on how it differs from regular feudal rulerdom in the long run.

What I can do instead is tell you a bit about the fun of council votes. The same pool of voters who in a republic like Venice, get a say in who succeeds the ruler, also vote on the passage of laws and decrees. One proposal you can put forward is a vote to change who exactly is allowed a seat in this voting pool. It defaults to just being heads of patrician families, but can be extended to include all vassals, or tightened up so only the Doge’s councillors or the ruler themselves have a say, that being the way despotism lies. As you can imagine, passing a change to who can vote can drastically change the state of play, either tightening up the number of folks who might oppose or support you, or bringing new folks into play in a fashion that dilutes individual power, but gives you more pieces on the board to mind or manipulate to your advantage.

I’ve found it suitably tough to orchestrate successful votes to change laws and customs which medieval Italian noble families, expectedly, have firmly entrenched stances on. Getting rid of checks and balances, such as the requirement to vote on banishments or wars - so the Doge can rule as a despot - has proven one such challenge, as has changing laws governing men being prioritised over women. I tried to pass equal succession as a substitute for men being put first while playing as Speronella, but met an insurmountable wall of resistance due to the region’s culture and faith. So, all I could do was try to put my young male heir in the best position possible to make the sorts of gains I couldn’t.

Much easier to weasel into place, either through some canny swaying or the offering of hooks, are laws giving state backing or other priority to trading in certain types of goods. Alcohol, for instance, which certainly hasn’t hurt the profits of Marco’s two wine trade routes.

Thus, cash continues to flow through the tentacles of my trade empire in sizable globs. As he’s now Doge, I’ve got Marco using the ample funds of Venice’s treasury to build a upcoming piazza and have him focused on making the city’s already-strong trade league even more formidable, by attracting new members from the few other northern Italian blocs.

It has been revealed that while I’m fairly sure there are folks who’ll find Silk and Silver's constant barrage of trade route notifications annoying, or that their power-grabbing skills and sheer multitude of money-making means combine to make playthroughs less challenging than they could be, so far I've found it another enjoyably sonorous string to Crusader Kings 3’s bow. Above all else, playing as a merchant gives more reason to invest in stewardship skills beyond just maximising your tax yields, while the republican politics of the DLC's main region fleshes out rewarding intrigue-focused builds. Diplomacy and martial skills are less key, but still have their place at times.

If you’re an absolute stickler for historical accuracy, you may well find other things to gripe about, but aside from the Guelph and Ghibelline conflict fading into the background, I’ve found plenty to like in my quest to become top Doge.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 21-year-old responsible for hacking Rockstar Games and leaking in-development GTA 6 footage in 2022 has pleaded guilty to a number of offenses.

Industry observers note that the GTA 6 leaker was initially sentenced to an indefinite stay at a hospital due to his severe autism, but was more recently deemed fit for trial and moved to a regular prison earlier this January. On Monday, at the Woolwich Crown Court in South East London, he pleaded guilty to hacking Rockstar Games and a number of other companies, including Uber and EE/BT, in cyber attacks estimated to have caused £10m in damages.

At the time of his Rockstar hack - when he was between the ages of 16 and 17 - the leaker was already under police protection at a Travelodge hotel to keep him from rival hackers he had allegedly stolen Bitcoin from. Somewhat surprisingly, he then managed to hack the multi-billion dollar game maker with nothing but an Amazon Fire Stick, the hotel room's TV and a bluetooth-connected keyboard and mouse.

Industry observers note that as the BBC reports, he also managed to break into the developer's Slack channels, before threatening to release the GTA 6 source code if Rockstar failed to contact him within the day. The leaker has yet to be sentenced.

Recent findings suggest that those 2022 leaks were quite substantial, too, revealing about an hour of unfinished gameplay and clueing the world in on Lucia's existence - the series' first female protagonist in years. Of course, those 2022 leaks shouldn't be confused with 2026's, which saw Cyberleek spill nuggets of nearly finished clips onto the internet, despite Rockstar's best efforts to keep GTA 6 a closely guarded secret.

"We recently suffered a network intrusion in which an unauthorised third-party illegally accessed and downloaded confidential information from our systems, including early development footage for the next Grand Theft Auto," Rockstar said at the time, before it had officially unveiled GTA 6. "At this time we do not anticipate any disruption to our live game services, nor any long-term effect on the development of our ongoing projects. We are extremely disappointed to have any details of our next game shared with you all in this way.".

Four years later, GTA 6 is finally around the corner - you're probably already aware considering the marketing frenzy Rockstar's been drumming up.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • GTA 6 has been censored to a fairly large extent in Japan, where the country's strict ratings system often sees nudity, sexual content, and graphic violence be toned down or removed entirely in video games.
  • To be clear, GTA 6 has been given Japan's highest 18+ age rating — but it's still had to make changes in order to ensure its release in the region.
  • For starters, Rockstar's latest is packed with full-on nudity — to a degree never before seen in a mainstream release — but in Japan, it's apparently impossible to remove the underwear of main characters Jason and Lucia, even when they're taking a shower.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 has been censored to a fairly large extent in Japan, where the country's strict ratings system often sees nudity, sexual content, and graphic violence be toned down or removed entirely in video games.

To be clear, GTA 6 has been given Japan's highest 18+ age rating — but it's still had to make changes in order to ensure its release in the region.

For starters, Rockstar's latest is packed with full-on nudity — to a degree never before seen in a mainstream release — but in Japan, it's apparently impossible to remove the underwear of main characters Jason and Lucia, even when they're taking a shower.

The same is true of NPCs — everyone's always wearing at least one layer to cover up their privates.

Sources indicate that needless to say, the game's numerous sex scenes have also been censored. Again, it's a case of keeping clothes on — but some specific scenes have actually been cut completely.

Violence is next on the list. GTA 6 obviously features a lot of bloodshed but it's also rather gory, with accurate depictions of dismemberment and lethal physical trauma. It can all come across as particularly gruesome given how realistic the game looks.

Industry observers note that in Japan, it seems as though most of this stuff is scaled back. There's less blood spray in general, and spilled blood doesn't stay in place very long.

It's a little unclear just how far this censorship of violence goes, but it's not uncommon for Japan to remove things like dismemberment — especially if a game's got a grounded setting.

Sources indicate that for what it's worth, GTA 6 does have several settings that let you change the amount of blood and gore that's on display. I assume that in Japan, these settings are applied at a censored standard by default.

Industry observers note that interestingly, though, drug use seemingly hasn't been touched. Japan's got very strict anti-drug laws, but illegal goods are still totally usable in GTA 6.

Did you see this censorship coming? Try not to go on a blood-soaked rampage in the comments section below.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that split-screen racing comes as part of an entirely newly introduced mode called Free Play that'll also allow players to mix and match vehicles, characters, tracks and planets in a galaxy far, far away.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The surprisingly awesome arcade podracing game Star Wars: Galactic Racer is getting split-screen multiplayer next year after loud fan requests, developer Fuse Games has declared.

Recent findings suggest that split-screen racing comes as part of an entirely newly introduced mode called Free Play that'll also allow players to mix and match vehicles, characters, tracks and planets in a galaxy far, far away. So, maybe don't expect to bring friends into the game's vast, pre-existing suite of modes just yet.

According to recent reports, "We heard you," the studio wrote on social media. "Local split-screen multiplayer racing is coming in early 2027. A dedicated team at Fuse Games has been working hard to bring a brand latest mode, Free Play, to Star Wars: Galactic Racer. This new mode will allow you to choose your vehicle, character, planet, and race track to race alone or with up to 3 other players in local split-screen action.".

We’ve heard you! Local split-screen multiplayer racing is coming in early 2027. A dedicated team at @Fuse_Games has been working hard to bring a brand new mode, Free Play, to STAR WARS: Galactic Racer™. This new mode will allow you to choose your vehicle, character, planet, and race track to race alone or with up to 3 other players in local split-screen action.

Galactic Racer already has a pretty good selection of online multiplayer modes, like the 12-player speeder races and 8-player podracing tours, but there's presently no way to play with your mates in the same room.

Sources indicate that chris Donlan loved the thrilling racing game for mixing the best bits of Star Wars and Burnout - Fuse Games does have plenty of old Criterion DNA, mind you. "It's newly introduced games, with Roguelite choices and endless unlockables, and it's also old games, with cruel and ingenious courses where everything can be lost in an instant. It's a Galaxy Far, Far Away, and it's also Paradise City," he wrote in Eurogamer's five-star review.

With Galactic Racer and Zero Tech giant under its belt, Lucasfilm Games said it's now "more flexible" about which developers it accepts pitches from. Hopefully, that'll lead to even more interesting games set in Star Wars' ultra flexible world.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • New multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five.
  • Industry observers note that deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities.
  • Recent findings suggest that there's nothing forcing you to do any of this in tech giant, mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five. By default, players appear to each other as shadows, all exploring a skybound landscape of magic animals and layer-cake mountains that reminds me of both Sable and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

Industry observers note that deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities. For example, going fishing, playing instruments round the campfire, playing dress-up and pulling emotes in group photos, bouncing around on strangely inflated yaks, or questing forth to heal troubled spirits. There's some material gathering and crafting, and there are recurring storms that make the ambience more threatening, but overcoming a challenge doesn't feel like the point of Spirit Crossing. The "missions" are just an excuse to hang out together.

Recent findings suggest that there's nothing forcing you to do any of this in tech giant, mind. "Stay a mysterious shadow, lend a hand when you feel like it, and disappear before anyone can make it weird," the devs explain, adding a hug emoji to make plain that they don't think you're some kind of smelly misanthrope for shunning other players.

I, personally, am a smelly misanthrope, and will only ever appear in your game as a skulking opacity, peering through the window of your personal gingerbread house, with its tastefully accessorised lava lamps and throw rugs. No, I will not join you for a group hang-glider tour. No, I do not want to play the banjo with you. You will experience me only as the nagging sensation of being watched, while you chat to the local "Stylesmith" about fetching rucksack patterns.

Spirit Crossing has an upfront cost that "gives players full access to the complete game experience in perpetuity", but you can also take out a subscription for some cosmetic items and access to a "limited resource exchange shop". They're avoiding traditional microtransactions, which is nice.

Spry Fox are also the developers of Cozy Grove - "the best grove since Byker", wrote Graham, in one of his regular 'senior moments'. I myself know them as the studio behind wintry puzzler Road Not Taken, with its randomised woodlands, and block-merging city builder Triple Town, with its unexpectedly terrifying bears. Little about Spirit Crossing seems terrifying, unless you count the shadow loitering at the edge of your conversation pit.

It has been revealed that you can read more about the game on Steam. I find Spirit Crossing quite novel, especially when it dispenses with the WholeCosy "discover your inner fashonista" stuff and leans into the supernatural elements: I like the idea of hunkering by the campfire during a storm, watching the clouds hurtle past. Still, I'm disappointed to hear that Spry Fox have made use of generative AI during its creation.

As has been pointed out to us on Bluesky, the developers called on Anthropic's Claude tools for various behind-the-scenes tasks - the example they give in a Discord post is editing several config files at once. There's no disclosure on the game's Steam page because Spry Fox haven't used AI tools to generate any of the art or music - Valve rewrote Steam's disclosure requirements in January to exempt the usage of generative AI for "efficiency gains", which the above presumably falls under.

It's hardly a full-throated endorsement of generative AI, but it still forms part of a political and cultural project I consider reckless and morbid. For a longer account of my objections, albeit one that doesn't cover Claude in particular, here's my longform thinkywangle from July last year.

#86539. Latest Update: Microsoft's SideWinder Strategic Commander was a failed attempt to reimagine RTS controls. 23 years later, why are some players still using it?

AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Microsoft's SideWinder Strategic Commander was a failed attempt to reimagine RTS controls. 23 years later, why are some players still using it?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1501 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • PC players have been conditioned for decades to accept the keyboard-and-mouse setup for RTS games.
  • Recent findings suggest that unveiled on March 1st 2000 at Microsoft's Gamestock event, the Strategic Commander was one of three additions to their SideWinder line, with a scheduled release that October at a pricey $64.95.
  • Microsoft, all the while, were taking notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PC players have been conditioned for decades to accept the keyboard-and-mouse setup for RTS games. One hand has to handle movement and commands through a keyboard, while the other points, drags, and selects with a mouse. Peripheral makers have, usually with the addition of more buttons, made many minor variations to this time-honored arrangement, but there's only ever been one real attempt to rethink it entirely for the PC: the Microsoft SideWinder Strategic Commander.

Recent findings suggest that unveiled on March 1st 2000 at Microsoft's Gamestock event, the Strategic Commander was one of three additions to their SideWinder line, with a scheduled release that October at a pricey $64.95. At E3 later that May, Microsoft demonstrated the Strategic Commander for the first time with SimCity 3000, while promoting its potential for other such games as Diablo II, Warcraft III, and Baldur's Gate II. This was all taking place during the so-called 'Golden Age of Real-Time Strategy Games,' which spanned roughly from the mid-1990s to the mid-2000s. It was when the RTS genre was at the peak of its mainstream popularity, and we fans were devoted to mastering its intricacies in any way we could to have a competitive edge.

Microsoft, all the while, were taking notes. "The team conceived the Strategic Commander in the late 1990s," Carl Ledbetter - then Industrial Design Manager for Microsoft's PC Hardware Group, now Head of Design for Xbox Devices - recalls to me. "As RTS games grew in popularity, we saw an interesting opportunity to design a upcoming physical interface around a new interaction model. The idea was for it to be used left-handed in concert with right-hand PC desktop mouse control. We wanted to enable players to perform faster with more fluidity, comfort, optimised control placement for multiple hand sizes, simplicity of set-up, and ease of programming.".

Industry observers note that for Ledbetter and co. to realise this ambition, the Strategic Commander was designed as a unique combination of mouse, joystick, and gamepad. To manage the increasing complexities of the RTS games of the day, it came equipped with six programmable buttons, three shift buttons, and a three-position profile switch. Back then, these atypical features provided an unprecedented 72 possible key combinations across various configurations, all at the tip of our stubby little fingers. Better yet, it allowed us to toggle between three pre-configured profiles at a time, so that we could switch up our configurations on the fly depending on which stage of an RTS match we were in.

On release, contemporary reviewers acknowledged its originality, with critics like ActiveWin's Julien Jay describing it as "probably the most innovative (with the GameVoice) and revolutionary" peripheral designed specifically for strategy players. Others, like Neoseeker's Arnel Lim, suggested that it might’ve gone overboard with its customisation options, saying "you won't use anywhere close to all of them," in reference to the controller's programmable key combinations. Either way, the Strategic Commander failed to supplant conventional peripherals in the hands of most RTS players, and it was discontinued in 2003. As was the rest of the original SideWinder line, owing to declining sales and the industry-wide shift toward standard M+K setups for all PC games and genres.

In a recent development, however, unlike so many of its Microsoft-made siblings, this was not the end for the Strategic Commander. Niche as it was, it went on to enjoy a surprisingly long post-shelf life, one that was stretched out by a dedicated cult following - and that continues to this day. But why? Why, after all these years, is this forgotten peripheral from a discontinued line maintaining such a enthusiastic fanbase, years after the industry around it had written it off as a failure?

The answer lies in software and OS compatibility, as much as the hardware's own appeal. Andreas Weis was the developer of one of the first unofficial patches for the Strategic Commander, allowing players to keep on using it even after the original software stopped being compatible with newer versions the Windows. By that point, the device was a decade old, and well into 'official' obsolescence, yet Weis still answered the call of the Strategic Commander's righteously frustrated - if numerically few - fans. "There was a lot of interest back in the early 2010s in software patches to keep the Strategic Commander functional when the original software for the Strategic Commander stopped working," he explains. "Users were asking around on internet forums about how to get it to work on Windows 7 and Vista machines. Since I was studying computer science at the time, I was quite interested in reverse-engineering, and I hacked together a simple tool that would cover my use cases for the device.".

Recent findings suggest that in the years that followed, other patches were released to keep the Strategic Commander operational, the most notable of which was Philip Merwarth’s Strategic Engine software in 2013. Unfortunately, they weren’t open-source. Worse was that the protocol for programming the Strategic Commander wasn’t documented anywhere online in a way that was accessible for owners. This is why Weis realized that he could make a unique contribution.

Recent findings suggest that "I polished my old prototype code for the Strategic Commander software patch and released it as a library, so that other people could use it to write their own applications for programming the tool," he states. "As for me, I released one application that made use of the library publicly, the vJoy feeder application, which allows the device to be used with games that support joystick inputs." Curiously, Weis, by this time and like many others, had found other applications for a device with such a specific selling point, and even continues to use the Strategic Commander sparingly in 2026.

"The production quality of Microsoft hardware at the time was just top-notch, and I love the design of the old SideWinder devices, which is why I did not just throw the thing out when the software stopped working," he tells me. "It was worth keeping around to find upcoming uses for it over the years, and I eventually realized that it makes quite a nice addition to a HOTAS (Hands-On Throttle And Stick) setup, where I could put actions that aren’t time-critical and don't fit well on the throttle on the Strategic Commander instead. For example, when I’m playing Elite Dangerous in VR, I’d put actions like deploying the landing gear on the Strategic Commander to free up buttons on the throttle for actions that were more relevant for combat.".

When looking back at the history of Microsoft’s SideWinder line, it’s easy to call the Strategic Commander a failed experiment, given the fact that most of us are still using the same standard mouse-and-keyboard setup to play RTS games. However, the central premise behind its design philosophy was that the interface between a player and a game could be redesigned to cater to specific genre quirks, and decades following its release, it’s still maintained a coalition of loyal users: some RTS players who believed the Strategic Commander really pulled it off, and those found other uses for the device in other flavours of PC game. And with the issue of modern compatibility, a roadblock for so much retro hardware, bypassed by homemade patches, both camps can continue twisting and clicking their Strategic Commanders unimpeded.

All the same, I wonder if it might have basked in more conventional success, had Microsoft made more forward-thinking decisions. The Strategic Commander has proven over the years that its unprecedented customisation had applications far beyond what Ledbetter’s team had envisioned, and once the popularity of RTS games settled down, other, similar click-heavy subgenres like MOBAs and Real-Time Tactics got massive as well. Would a more officially maintained, potentially refined Strategic Commander model have served those crowds? I think it might. The narrow focus on RTS games may have also hurt the device's since-demonstrated broader appeal; if Microsoft had fully capitalised on this customisation selling point by communicating its benefits to everyone, not just those playing the single most popular PC genre at the time, it could have provided the blueprint for a proper, long-lived alternative to controllers, mice, and keyboards.

It has been revealed that alas, gaming history is littered with revolutionary peripherals that failed to actually revolutionise the industry surrounding them. The Strategic Commander is no different, but for the fact that it’s had this surprisingly long post-shelf life - and, as a result, the opportunity for insight into what could have been done to salvage the its failures. Still, that unexpected longevity can provide come comfort to the Strategic Commander's creators, as well as its lingering people.

"I think the design made sense for its time, especially with the rising popularity of RTS games," Ledbetter reflects. "Looking back, I would have liked more time to test and refine the Strategic Commander. I’m proud of what we brought to market, and I’m glad to know that it remains beloved by many players to this day.".

  • According to recent reports, the trio of companies deny having colluded, arguing in a latest motion to have the case dismissed (thanks, IGN) that this suit simply retreads old ground covered in a previous antitrust case and quoting deceased judge Richard Posner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A judge has denied a motion to dismiss a US lawsuit against chip makers Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron. The suit acccuses the companies of fixing RAM prices and supply, thereby contributing to worsening the effects of the ongoing memory crisis.

The class action suit was filed at the United States District Court for the Northern District of California in June this year. It accuses Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron of moving in lockstep away from production of consumer-focused DDR3 and DDR4 RAM and towards HBM memory more typically used in AI datacenters. The suit claims that "in a competitive commodity market", "at least one of three large producers, seeing record prices, would expand output of the product whose price was rising", thereby forcing their competitors to either follow suit or risk losing out on customers.

According to recent reports, the trio of companies deny having colluded, arguing in a latest motion to have the case dismissed (thanks, IGN) that this suit simply retreads old ground covered in a previous antitrust case and quoting deceased judge Richard Posner. "[C]ompetitors in concentrated markets watch each other like hawks," was the Posner quote they wheeled out, which I mention because otherwise the response I'm about to lay out will sound like a very weird tangent.

Sources indicate that "But Plaintiffs’ allegations go beyond hawks watching each other," judge Noël Wise wrote in her order to deny the dismissal motion. "Their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation – an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do.".

In a recent development, you know a case is getting serious when facts about Avian behaviour start being wheeled out in response to similes. Bird chatter aside, all this decision means is that the case will rumble on, with both sides still having a chance to present more evidence or make points in their favour before any eventual decision is made by the courts.

So, shelve any hopes you might have of a rapid solution to the memory crisis, which right now looks likely to last until at least 2028.

"Don't let 210GB get between you and your league," the post reads, clearly quoting GTA 6's file size.

The update in question is fairly notable, adding a Madden 97 throwback with era-appropriate players, playbooks and what looks to be 16-bit visuals. Though it's obviously not related to GTA 6 in any way, it's easy to see why EA would fear a significant drop in players once Rockstar's game arrives, something other publishers are undoubtedly worried about.

Industry observers note that as part of a recent restructuring, EA laid off 400 employees, closed down BioWare, cancelled unannounced projects and revealed a refocusing on its core franchises and biggest monkey-makers.
